title: The Minimal Groups
text:
Around 1970, Henri Tajfel and his colleagues at the University of Bristol wanted to find the least it takes to make people favor their own group. They worked with teenage boys from a local school who already knew one another.

In one version, the boys looked at slides of abstract paintings by Paul Klee and Wassily Kandinsky and said which they preferred. Each boy was then told, privately, that he belonged to the Klee group or the Kandinsky group. In truth the assignment was essentially random. The boys never met their fellow group members, did not know who they were, and gained nothing personally from the task that followed.

Each boy then sat alone and divided small sums of real money between two other boys, identified only by code numbers and group labels. He never allocated money to himself. The researchers used carefully built tables of choices that let them see which strategy each boy preferred.

The boys consistently gave more to members of their own group. More surprising, many chose options that maximized the gap between their group and the other one, even when that meant their own group got less in absolute terms than another choice would have given it. A label based on a taste in paintings was enough to create rivalry.
lesson: Teams form an us and a them out of almost nothing. When you draw lines between departments or squads, expect favoritism and work on purpose to keep the larger shared goal in view.
people: Henri Tajfel, Michael Billig, R. P. Bundy, Claude Flament
source: Tajfel, H., Billig, M. G., Bundy, R. P., and Flament, C. (1971). Social categorization and intergroup behaviour. European Journal of Social Psychology, 1(2), 149-178.
place: University of Bristol, Wills Memorial Building, UK
